subject: english-language
title: Formal and Informal
welcome_lead: Speech changes when the audience changes. Learn the levels.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on formal and informal register.
final_note: You can now flex register for context and audience.

walkthroughs.body_html: A job interview needs formal register; a chat with friends uses informal register. Both can be 'correct' for context.
Codeswitching is shifting between language varieties — from dialect to standard, or one language to another, mid-conversation.
Real speech is full of fillers ('um', 'like'), tag questions ('right?') and discourse markers ('so'). They organise live talk.

mcqs.q: Switching between language varieties is called.

options: Implicature is a kind of grammatical mistake.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
Meaning conveyed beyond what is literally said — generated when speakers obey or deliberately flout Grice's maxims. 'Some students passed' implicates 'not all', via the maxim of quantity.
Implicature is the same as the literal meaning of a sentence.
Alternating between languages or varieties within a conversation or even a single utterance — often patterned by context, topic, identity or audience. Code-switching is rule-governed, not random.
Code-switching shows the speaker doesn't know either language properly.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
Code-switching means using slang words in formal speech.
Implicature is a kind of grammatical mistake.
A syntactic unit headed by a noun, which may include determiners, adjectives and modifiers — e.g. 'the big red car' is a noun phrase functioning as a single grammatical unit.
A noun phrase is just a noun by itself.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
